summary.text: 回 is a whole graph associated with turning or circular motion. Its exact early referent is uncertain; common uses include “return” and counting an occurrence.

formation.text: The graph is best treated as a pictograph of a spiral or revolving form. One interpretation specifies water turning in a circle, but the depicted object and exact original meaning remain uncertain. A competing proposal treats 回 and 囘 as originally distinct graphs and words, with 回 meaning “around”; their relationship is unresolved. No separate semantic or phonetic parts within 回 are established.

components.text: 回 is represented as one whole picture associated with a spiral or circular motion. The traditional description of an outer 囗 and an inner revolving shape is an account of its appearance, not proof that these are independent components.

history.text: Historical accounts describe circular or revolving forms and label examples as oracle-bone, bronze, seal, and clerical script. These labels do not establish a verified sequence of graphic changes.

The traditional account describes an outer 囗 enclosing a shape resembling rotation. A competing proposal treats 囘 and 回 as originally distinct graphs and words, suggesting 回 was made for “around” and modeled on 圍. Their relationship remains unresolved.

In 迴, 回 is reported as a sound-and-meaning component. The two graphs share Mandarin huí and have corresponding historical readings in the cited reconstruction systems; this compound role does not establish a phonetic part in 回’s own origin.

uncertainties.text: The spiral or circular-motion interpretation is supported, but the depicted object and exact earliest meaning remain uncertain. The competing distinction between 囘 and 回 cannot be fully assessed from the available account.

The earliest attested sense and any chronology linking turning, returning, replying, and occurrence-counting have not been established. Dictionary glosses and literary examples do not by themselves show that sequence.
The proposed derivation of the ethnonym 回回 from Uyghur or Old Turkic forms remains unverified; the source word and historical sound match are uncertain.
The sound relationship between 回 and 迴 is supported, but when 迴 arose or when the graphs became variant or distributionally distinct spellings is unresolved.

senses.text: Turning or revolving is proposed as the graph’s early meaning, but no securely dated contextual occurrence establishes it as the earliest attested sense.
“Return” is a common current meaning. Its historical relationship to the turning sense is unresolved.
回 can refer to one time or occurrence and serve as a counter. The evidence does not date this use or show how it developed.

limitations.text: The available examples and glosses do not establish the chronology or semantic pathway connecting turning, returning, and occurrence-counting uses.

The proposed 回回 ethnonym borrowing is a separate account of a word written with this graph, not evidence of a semantic development from 回. The proposed source and sound-based borrowing remain unverified.

components.text: Read 回 as one whole picture associated with circular motion; its outer and inner shapes are not established as separate meaning-bearing parts.

relationships.text: Turning or revolving is proposed as the graph’s early meaning, but no securely dated contextual occurrence establishes it as the earliest attested sense.

evidence.text: Originally, a spiral signifying return
Originally a spiral, conveying the meaning "to turn around".
轉也。从囗，中象回轉形。
Pictogram (象形): rotation (originally a spiral).
From earlier name 回回 (huíhuí), variant of 回鶻／回鹘 (Huíhú), from either Old Uyghur 𐽳𐽶𐽲𐽳𐽾 (wyqwr) or Old Turkic 𐰆𐰖𐰍𐰺 (uygur). Doublet of 維吾爾／维吾尔 (Wéiwú'ěr).

For pronunciation and definitions of 回 – see 迴 (“to revolve; to rotate; to avoid; etc.”).
(This character is the simplified and variant form of 迴).
 Notes:
Simplified Chinese is mainly used in Mainland China, Malaysia, and Singapore.
Traditional Chinese is mainly used in Hong Kong, Macau, and Taiwan.

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

search_audit.query: 回 Baxter–Sagart exact reading and 迴 component sound readings; Hanyu character dictionary component roles 辶 回
search_audit.outcome: Inspected 迴’s compound analysis and phonological entries. These distinguish its 辶 semantic component and 回 sound/meaning component from hypotheses about 回’s own formation.

gaps: No primary inscription image or contextual oracle-bone/bronze occurrence was inspected; the claim that 回 is attested in Shang oracle script is reported by a secondary character page, not independently verified against a corpus entry.

The proposed spiral/water-rotation depiction is plausible and repeated by the inspected Dong Chinese entry, but the specific physical referent and its exact original meaning are not established by the inspected evidence. No distinct semantic component can be identified: 囗 and the inner strokes are the graphic parts described in Shuowen’s account, while the account itself is not proof of original segmentation.

No securely dated textual examples were inspected to establish the order of senses such as turn/return, answer, classifier for occurrences, or chapter/section. A dictionary’s bundled glosses do not establish chronology.

No evidence was found in inspected pages for the dossier’s 回回 ethnonym derivation or the proposed Uyghur/Old Turkic source. That proposed whole-word/ethnonym loan is separate from 回’s graphic origin and from 回 serving as a sound component; the source word’s early attestation and historical pronunciation remain unverified here.

No dated evidence was inspected for when 回 and 迴 became variant or distributionally distinct spellings. The compound 迴 is reported as semantic 辶 plus phonetic 回 in the dossier, and the sound series and matching readings support the phonetic relationship, but no independent early compound inscription was examined.

The local structured B-S rows checked were 回 U+56DE, *[ɢ]ʷˤəj / hwoj and 迴 U+8FF4, *[ɢ]ʷˤəj / hwoj. No discrepancy with the secondary B-S transcription was found; Zhengzhang *ɡuːl and *ɡuːls are a separate system and scope, not a correction to B-S.

No invocation-supplied xiaoxuetang_query candidate forms were provided. A direct character-specific query could not be retrieved, so no Xiaoxuetang image is selected despite verification of its CC0 notice.

No usable image with both a verified 回-specific identity and clear reuse rights was established. Dong Chinese labels candidate historical forms but image fetches failed with cache misses and its page does not state image rights. The Commons image is explicitly a vector tracing of a specific oracle-bone inscription but does not identify it as 回. The CUHK image link also failed to fetch and its reuse rights are not stated.

No primary artifact image or primary inscription context for a securely dated early occurrence of 回 was inspected. The page labels and scholarly accounts attribute early forms, but they do not independently demonstrate the graph in a dated inscription context here.

The physical referent and exact early semantic value of the proposed spiral or water-rotation depiction remain uncertain. The circular/rotation account is supported by multiple modern reference pages, while Wu Kejing’s article abstract argues a distinction between 囘 ‘whirl’ and 回 ‘around’; the full article was behind a download captcha, so that analysis could not be evaluated in detail.

The CUHK page cites Classic of Poetry and other classical examples, but exact composition dates and earliest attestations for senses such as return, reply, classifier, avoidance, or section/chapter were not independently established. Its examples are not a complete chronology.

The dossier’s proposed 回回 ethnonym derivation from Uyghur/Old Uyghur or Old Turkic was not pursued to independently verifiable early attestations of both source and borrowed word in this set. No claim is made here about the origin or historical pronunciation of the source ethnonym.

The research supports 回 as a sound/meaning component of 迴, but dates for when the compound arose or when 回 and 迴 became variant/distributionally distinct spellings were not established. B–S *[ɢ]ʷˤəj is recorded for the 迴 phonological row; the matching broad comparison does not prove a phonetic role in 回’s original formation.

No separate semantic and phonetic components within 回 itself are securely established. Shuowen’s outer 囗/inner shape description is preserved as a historical account, while the alternative article treats distinct old graphs/words; neither establishes a separate phonetic component.

limitations.text: No candidate glyph image is available to select. The historical shape accounts describe circular or revolving forms, but the exact object depicted and the graph’s earliest meaning remain uncertain.
